title: SpaceX Eyes Orbital AI Compute as Starship Reuse Pushes Costs Lower
excerpt: SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) CFO Bret Johnsen outlined the company’s strategy across reusable launch systems, satellite connectivity and artificial intelligence infr...
content_html:
Key Points

  • Interested in SpaceX? Here are five stocks we like better.

  • Starship reuse is a key cost-reduction goal: Flight 13 demonstrated improved vehicle performance, while Flight 14 will carry production Starlink satellites. SpaceX plans to attempt recovery of both stages later this year, potentially lowering satellite deployment costs.

  • SpaceX is expanding into orbital AI computing: The company targets its first orbital-compute satellite launches next year and believes the technology could reach cost parity with terrestrial data centers as Starship reuse improves. It also plans to increase terrestrial compute capacity from just over 2 gigawatts to 5–10 gigawatts next year.

  • Connectivity businesses continue to broaden: Starlink is pursuing enterprise and mobility customers across more than 170 countries, while next-generation direct-to-device satellites could deliver full 5G-quality service beginning in the first half of 2028.

  • AST SpaceMobile Looks to Extend Its 30-Day FCC Satellite Testing Window

SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) CFO Bret Johnsen outlined the company's strategy across reusable launch systems, satellite connectivity and artificial intelligence infrastructure, emphasizing vertical integration as a central operating principle.

Speaking at an investor conference, Johnsen said the company's approach extends from rocket manufacturing and satellite production to customer relationships, terrestrial computing infrastructure and planned orbital computing systems.

→ IBM and Lockheed Martin Turn a Swiss Defense Deal Into a Quantum Computing Bet

  • 3 Stocks Built for Higher Rates—And 2 That Could Break

"We really believe that we are building the infrastructure of the future," Johnsen said. He said the company adopted vertical integration early in its rocket and spacecraft operations because it could not find supply-chain providers moving at the pace or meeting the quality standards it required.

Starship milestones and reuse plans

Johnsen described Starship as central to the company's businesses, including satellite broadband, direct-to-device mobile service and orbital computing. He said Flight 13 delivered demonstration V3 satellites, included a Raptor engine relight and achieved what he called the second stage's "softest" and most precise ocean splashdown to date.

The company recovered the vehicle after the splashdown, allowing engineers to inspect it and assess how the heat shield performed, he said. Those findings are being incorporated into preparations for Flight 14 and subsequent missions.
